boundaries: how many times a send asks the server for the group key state
which key version a sender seals under
the refusal when a member has published no usable key
whether a control patch is still evidence after the file it targets changes

prior_ledgers_read: da9ed20de -- the cache this phase extends. Its findings were a suite that mocked what it claimed to prove, and a required call nothing enforced. Both shaped how this phase was tested.
0efe747b3 -- the display rule that consumes these keys; its findings came from printing what the rule returns rather than reading it, which is the move that found this phase's first defect too.
b28df65f3 -- g1d: a stored public key is guaranteed non-empty, never usable. That is why groupKeyForSending refuses on an unusable member key rather than skipping the member.
af4bacefe -- g1c: a required call that no test reached, so a later edit could drop it unseen.
cd683f853 -- g2a: vectors pinned in one direction only.
notes: Both findings came from printing what the code does rather than reading it. The first was a table of what groupKeyForSending does in each situation, which showed two state fetches where one was needed. The second came from re-applying every control after refactoring a file they target.

The same table showed two things that are unreachable rather than broken, and they are recorded here rather than fixed. Rotating an empty set of copies needs a group with no members, but groupMembers lists participants of a conversation the caller must belong to and State refuses a non-member, so a successful fetch always contains the sender: the probe only produced it because the mock returned an empty member list beside a successful fetch, which the server cannot do. A member holding no copy of a current version needs a damaged copy, because MarkGroupKeyStale clears is_active on every join and leave and active_version is the newest active row.

Priming the cache on every send discards that reader's record of versions it cannot open. Measured rather than assumed: two asks for an unopenable version cost one fetch, and after a send three more asks cost two. So a send costs one extra fetch, not one per message, and the record rebuilds itself.

instruments.evidence: One function deciding which key a sender seals with, plus its suite. The boundary is how often the server is asked and which version is chosen.

instruments.evidence: The next version is latest_version + 1, and the value returned is the one the server stored, not the one requested.
The rotation body carries key_version and a copy per member, matching what GroupKeyRotation declares and what the handler binds.
The active-version path and the mint path are two routes to one answer; the table ran both and compared what each produced.

The control breaks the reader: it removes the priming so the cache must fetch again, and the one-fetch assertion fails.
Found a fixture that cannot occur: the probe's empty member list alongside a successful state fetch. The server cannot produce that, because State refuses a caller who is not in the member list.
A group with a usable active version, and a group with none, both produce a key to seal with.
An unusable member key refuses and rotates nothing; no device keys refuses before touching the network.
Version zero, a version this device cannot open, and losing the race are all covered.
The server refuses rotation when a member has published no key; the client refuses for the same reason rather than skipping that member, which is the rule b28df65f3 established.
Every branch is reachable except the two recorded as unreachable in the notes.
A refusal it cannot recover from is rethrown unchanged rather than flattened into a generic failure.
The subject of the finding: a send asked for the same state twice, which is one wasted round trip on every message after the first.
The unwrap loop is shared between the fetching path and the priming path rather than copied, because collapsing a duplicate of that exact loop was a finding in this module's own review.
Deferred the sweep for the same refetch shape to pass 2.
Two members sending at once is the ordinary case; the loser takes the winner's version rather than failing.
A refused rotation writes nothing, and the sender falls back to reading the winner's version.
forgetGroupKeys runs after every rotation, so the record of missing versions cannot outlive the grant that fixes it.
The fix is controlled, and the control produced a real assertion failure rather than a build break.
The rotation ratchet runs as an ordinary test on every run; it passes trivially for this file, which is why the forget call is proven by effect instead.
The control feeds the function the situation it must handle in one fetch, and the assertion refuses two.

findings.summary: A send fetched the group key state twice on the common path: once to decide whether the group had an active version, and again inside the cache on the miss that followed. That is one wasted round trip on every message after the first, which is the per-item request shape the cache review removed one phase earlier, reintroduced a layer up. The cache can now be seeded with a state the caller already holds.

Found the defect. Re-applying every control after refactoring groupKeyCache.ts showed one refused outright: git apply reported that the patch does not apply, because extracting unwrapCopies moved the line it targeted.

findings.summary: Extracting unwrapCopies out of openMyCopies during this review moved the line that the control for groupkeycache-unwrap-never-proven was written against, so git apply refused it. That control is the one showing a mocked suite could not see the private key swapped for the public one, and it had quietly stopped being evidence. A control that cannot apply proves as little as one that passes, and reads worse, because a refusal looks like a skip rather than a failure.

control.observed: Before the rebuild git apply reported: patch failed at groupKeyCache.ts:48, patch does not apply. After it, the patch applies and the mocked suite passes 11 of 11 while the real-crypto suite fails with expected null not to be null and a real TypeError from decrypt -- the signature it had when first built.
